concepts.title: The Reasonable Price and the Fatal Question
concepts.definition: Wole Soyinka's dramatic monologue opens with an African applicant finding a flat at a reasonable price, location indifferent, landlady off premises. The negotiation proceeds until he confesses, honestly, that he is African -- and the line falls silent before her careful, accentless voice returns with the fatal question: HOW DARK?
concepts.key_idea: One honest word -- African -- stops the civil transaction and starts the comedy of prejudice.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww114.txt opening lines (price seemed reasonable, landlady swore she lived off premises, confession of being african, silence, how dark)
question_patterns: what changes the tone of the telephone conversation
in class 11 telephone conversation: why does the narrator confess he is african
how does the landlady react to the word african
explain the significance of the silence on the telephone

why does the narrator say he hates a wasted journey

solution_steps.explain: Price agreed, location acceptable, everything businesslike -- the ritual of renting runs smoothly.
The narrator chooses honesty, announcing his African identity before wasting either party's journey.
The polite machinery seizes; her voice returns spelled out in cold capital letters: HOW DARK?

concepts.title: HOW DARK? -- The Telephone Inquisition
concepts.definition: The landlady presses: are you light or very dark? Clause by clause the narrator catalogues her question's absurdity -- is darkness a matter of 'down' in his person? He offers sarcastic measurements --Button B, Breast pocket, rcta -- treating skin as a telephone feature, exposing the indecency of the question by literalising it.
concepts.key_idea: Answering prejudice with satire -- the applicant measures his skin like a telephone part, and the question stands naked.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww114.txt central stanzas (light or very dark, button b breast pocket, rcta, peroxide blonde, spectroscopic measurement of colour)
question_patterns: what question does the landlady ask repeatedly and why
in class 11 telephone conversation: explain the narrator's sarcastic replies about button b and breast pocket
how does the narrator satirise the idea of measuring skin colour
what is meant by peroxide blonde and fringe in the poem
describe the landlady's voice as the poem portrays it
why does the narrator mention sepia, milk chocolate and brunette

solution_steps.explain: HOW DARK? -- ARE YOU LIGHT OR VERY DARK? -- the poem's central refrain of prejudice.
The narrator offers to read his colour off the phone's Button B or breast pocket, mocking the demand for measurement.
He lists absurd shades -- sepia, milk chocolate, brunette -- or offers to sit spectroscopically, turning science against silliness.

concepts.title: Madam, Wasn't It -- the Ending's Polite Fury
concepts.definition: The landlady, weakened, still clings to her manners: she invites him over if he is willing, backing it with her 'aren't you sure?' The narrator, holding the burning wire, answers with courteous venom: 'Madam, wasn't it my choosing / your choice of address' -- finishing the humiliation before slamming the receiver on her 'monstrous' politeness.
concepts.key_idea: Courtesy as a weapon -- the last polite exchange detonates the landlady's refined racism.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww114.txt closing lines (would you come, arent you sure, madam wasnt it my choosing, slamming the receiver, monstrous politeness)
question_patterns: what does the landlady offer at the end of the conversation
in class 11 telephone conversation: explain the narrator's final words to the landlady
why does the narrator thank the landlady sarcastically
how does the poem end and what does the ending suggest
who is dehumanised in the poem and how
is the landlady polite or monstrous discuss the contradiction

solution_steps.explain: Pressed by his mockery, the landlady falls back on etiquette -- do come, if you're sure.
He thanks her 'madam' for her 'monstrous' politeness and reverses the choosing: wasn't it his choice that decided?
He slams the receiver on her 'suffocating' civility -- the poem's anger sealed in courtesy.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the satire in the narrator's offer to 'sit down spectroscopically' for the landlady.

solution_template.explain: The landlady wants a precise shade -- light or very dark -- before consenting.
He offers a scientific demonstration of colour, as if skin were a specimen.
By over-obeying her absurd request, he exposes its absurdity -- racism measured is racism ridiculed.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does the narrator say 'I hate a wasted journey -- I am African'?

solution_template.explain: He chooses to disclose his identity before travelling, sparing himself a pointless trip.
Honesty up front also puts the landlady's prejudice to the test immediately.
The single sentence is both practical caution and principled self-declaration -- the hinge of the poem.
